LEAKSWEEP ENGINE CANARY — FAKE CREDENTIALS, NOT REAL SECRETS, NEVER ISSUED.

READ THIS BEFORE "FIXING" THE FILE.

Every string below is invented. None was ever minted, none grants access to
anything, and none may be removed, redacted, rotated, or "cleaned up". They are
here to be FOUND. On every single run, `leaksweep` plants this file into the tree
it is about to scan and requires both scanner engines to report it using their
OWN built-in rule sets — not our house rules. A run that reports nothing here has
not proved a clean tree; it has proved a dead scanner, and the sweep exits
non-zero and says so.

That distinction is the reason this file exists. This repository ran a P0
leak-on-main alerter that was silently dead for roughly 180 commits: it reported
nothing, and nothing is what a passing gate looks like. A gate with no canary
cannot tell "found no secrets" apart from "ran no rules".

The shapes below are chosen to trip stock detectors in both engines, so the proof
covers the maintained ecosystem rule sets we adopted these tools for, rather than
only the house config we wrote ourselves.

    aws_access_key_id     = __CANARY_AWS_ID__
    aws_secret_access_key = __CANARY_AWS_SECRET__
    slack_bot_token       = __CANARY_SLACK__

WHY THE PLACEHOLDERS, AND WHY THIS FILE IS NOT WEAKER FOR THEM
------------------------
The three fields above are filled in at RUN TIME by canary.go; the complete
credential shapes exist only in the temporary tree handed to the scanners, and
never as a literal in any tracked file.

This is not squeamishness, it is the resolution of a real tension. A canary has
to be realistic enough to trip a maintained scanner's stock rules — that is its
entire job — and anything that realistic also trips every OTHER secret guard it
passes on the way to review. This repository's own pre-write guard refused the
push twice while this fixture was being written, once on a GitHub token shape and
once on a cloud access-key ID. Both refusals were correct.

The wrong fixes were available and are worth naming, because both leave a gate
that reports success: override the guard (and teach everyone that this class of
refusal is noise), or water the canary down until no scanner reliably detects it.
A canary nobody detects is indistinguishable from a dead one.

So the shapes are assembled from fragments instead. The scanners see complete,
valid-looking credentials; the repository stores none. The assembly is one small
function with a test asserting each field is fully substituted, so a placeholder
that silently survives into the planted file is caught rather than shipped as a
canary that cannot fire.

If a scanner upgrade stops matching these shapes, the sweep will start failing
loudly with a dead-alerter message. That is the canary working. The fix is to add
a shape the new version does detect — never to relax the assertion.
